scores.evidence: Opening lede buries the verdict in scene-setting; 'hinged on a decision made while the cars were standing still' delays the evaluative claim
'He recovered the positions, made the tyres work and, when the race finally brought Russell within reach, completed the pass' — textbook summary restatement
'The race turned on lap 28' and 'Getting past was another matter' are bridging sentences doing transitional work that headings should handle
0.264 seconds, 0.85 seconds, 13.7 seconds, 3.857 seconds — figures cluster across consecutive paragraphs rather than deployed singly to clinch single claims
'His late-race pace suggests he would still have caught Russell rapidly' — 'suggests' is the only hedge; 'probably / I wonder if' markers absent throughout
Russell is the consistent benchmark for Antonelli throughout; gap in seconds to teammate anchors every phase of the race analysis
No quotes, radio messages, or official communications appear anywhere in the piece
'He passed his teammate with three laps remaining… The final move settled the race' — recaps sequence rather than interpreting meaning; narrative runs order throughout
'leaving the Monza crowd to find its celebration in an Italian driver winning for Mercedes' — one dry note; otherwise earnest and unironic throughout
No first person appears anywhere; no judgment calls or surprises flagged; the analyst is invisible, making it read as machine-neutral reportage
Names dropped without introduction, VSC jargon unexplained, chicane named without gloss — peer address maintained consistently
'During the early red flag… For much of the afternoon… Then a virtual safety car' — second paragraph makes three separate points without exiting
'A lap later, he was through' works well; but most paragraphs are uniformly medium-length with little visible sentence-length variation
VSC mechanism gets appropriate room but the closing section sprawls equally; coda ('Antonelli heads to Madrid') reads like a standings update, not a relaxed exit

top_fixes: Cut the final three paragraphs entirely — they restate the argument and add a standings summary that kills the piece twice; close on 'completed the pass' or, better, find a harder exit one beat earlier

Insert at least one radio clip or team message as evidentiary punctuation, and flag one genuine judgment call in first person (e.g. 'I'm not convinced Russell ever had a real answer once the VSC fired') to put an analyst on the page

Stop narrating sequence and start interpreting: replace 'He passed his teammate with three laps remaining' with what that pass revealed about the strategy call — the reader watched; they need meaning, not running order
